question: An analyst's first draft from Claude is vague, and she wonders whether she should move up to a deeper-reasoning tier to fix it. Which two responses are sound? Select two.
options: A) Escalate to the deepest tier right away, since depth is the usual cause of a weak first draft.
B) Stay on the lightest tier no matter what, because the tier has little effect on answer quality.
C) Check first whether the request was under-specified, since a deeper tier supplies no context.
D) Escalate the tier only when the work truly needs more reasoning depth than it is now getting.
E) Split the same request across three chats on three tiers and merge whichever parts look best.
correct_answers: C) Check first whether the request was under-specified, since a deeper tier supplies no context.
D) Escalate the tier only when the work truly needs more reasoning depth than it is now getting.
explanations: Incorrect. Reaching for the deepest tier as a reflex spends quota without fixing the under-specified request underneath.
Incorrect. The tiers do differ in reasoning depth, so refusing to escalate is as unexamined as escalating by default.
Correct. Vagueness most often comes from a thin prompt, and no tier can invent the audience, format or source material you left out.
Correct. Escalating is the right move when reasoning depth is genuinely the binding constraint, and only then.
Incorrect. Running the same weak prompt three times multiplies the cost and still leaves the original specification problem in place.
